provenance: Agent-assisted reconstruction from GitHub API records, not an OpenRouter extraction run. Every record remains needs_review. Quotes are deterministically validated before persistence.

candidates.title: Keep top-level convenience calls synchronous
candidates.claim: In the synchronous-support redesign, the maintainer chose a synchronous top-level convenience API and required an explicit client instance for asynchronous use. The proposed aget-style convenience names were not retained because they would not mirror the client methods.
candidates.scope: Historical API design discussion in #572; this reconstruction does not assert present-day API names or behavior.

evidence.quote: @florimondmanca made a good point about `aget()` etc not mirroring the client methods, so I think we'll just keep things really simple. Standard ol' thread-concurrency API for the top level convienence case, great with the REPL etc.
There's no good enough reason to support async without an explicit client instance.

alternatives.approach: Expose asynchronous top-level convenience calls such as aget()
alternatives.rationale: The proposed names would not mirror the client methods, and the maintainer saw no sufficient reason for async use without an explicit client.

evidence.quote: @florimondmanca made a good point about `aget()` etc not mirroring the client methods, so I think we'll just keep things really simple.
There's no good enough reason to support async without an explicit client instance.

candidates.title: Remove the synchronous facade over async internals
candidates.claim: The maintainer reported the removal released in 0.8, criticizing the existing sync approach for making the API and implementation poorer. A later comment in the same discussion pointed to #572 and a replacement based on regular synchronous calls and sockets rather than hidden async behavior.
candidates.scope: The removal and later proposed replacement of the historical sync bridge, not a claim that HTTPX currently lacks synchronous support.

evidence.quote: Done, and released as 0.8.
it's making the API & implementation significantly poorer.
We'll also be using regular ol' function calls and sync socket operations in the sync case, rather than hiding async stuff underneath a sync facade.

alternatives.approach: Keep the prior synchronous facade backed by async operations
alternatives.rationale: The maintainer considered the previous approach harmful to API and implementation quality.

evidence.quote: I'd can see us coming back to covering sync at a later date, but I just don't dig our approach onto it right now - it's making the API & implementation significantly poorer.

open_questions: The exact release that completed the replacement is not established by these excerpts.
possible_supersession: Issue #572 proposes a different synchronous implementation approach.

candidates.title: Reject global state for JSON customization
candidates.claim: The maintainer opposed JSON customization APIs that use global state. The stated concern was that installing a dependency could silently change another API client's JSON behavior at a distance.
candidates.scope: The global-state constraint expressed in #717; a non-global customization proposal remained distinct from an implemented feature.

evidence.quote: I can't see myself doing anything other than veto'ing proposals that use a form of global state
Installing a new dependancy to your project could end up altering the behaviour of an API client without that being visible anywhere obvious in the project codebase.

alternatives.approach: Set JSON handlers globally through a shared configuration function
alternatives.rationale: Global configuration could introduce distant, non-obvious changes to API client behavior when dependencies are installed.

evidence.quote: The issue with that approach is that you introduce subtly different JSON handling at a distance. Installing a new dependancy to your project could end up altering the behaviour of an API client without that being visible anywhere obvious in the project codebase.

open_questions: These excerpts do not establish that the alternative request/response-class proposal was implemented.

candidates.title: Own the custom transport API inside HTTPX
candidates.claim: The PR describes moving custom transport subclassing to HTTPX BaseTransport and AsyncBaseTransport, with a primitive low-level boundary that separates the HTTPX API from network handling. The maintainer explicitly endorsed proceeding with the change.
candidates.scope: Historical PR #1522. Its edited description explicitly incorporates follow-up #1550; this card does not claim the description is an untouched snapshot of the initial patch.

evidence.quote: You should either subclass `httpx.BaseTransport` to implement a transport to use with `Client`, or subclass `httpx.AsyncBaseTransport` to implement a transport to use with `AsyncClient`.
This strict point of cut-off provides a clear design separation between the HTTPX API, and the low-level network handling.
Ace, let's do this.

alternatives.approach: Document custom transports as subclasses of httpcore.SyncHTTPTransport
alternatives.rationale: The PR identified that exposed transport contract as the exception to treating httpcore as an implementation detail.

evidence.quote: Almost all the way through `httpcore` is treated as an implementation detail, that just happens to be used by the default transport implementation, `httpx.HTTPTransport`.
The one place where this isn't the case is in our "Transport API". In that case we're explicitly documenting "subclass httpcore.SyncHTTPTransport and implement it's API".

possible_supersession: PR #1550 is explicitly incorporated into the edited source description.

candidates.title: Replace rfc3986 with an internal URL parser
candidates.claim: The PR proposes removing the rfc3986 dependency in favor of an internal urlparse implementation. The author argued that removing indirection lowered overall complexity despite adding local code. A later maintainer comment judged the change ready and called for a version bump because it removes a dependency.
candidates.scope: The rationale and approval expressed in PR #2252; current parser behavior is not inferred from the historical discussion.

evidence.quote: This pull request drops the `rfc3986` package dependancy, in favour of a carefully worked through `urlparse` implementation, that provides everything we need in terms of URL validation and normalisation.
Although this adds some additional code, it also completely removes a dependancy, and is lower overall-complexity.
Looks ready to go from my side.
There's no breaking public API changes here, but since it removes a dependency I'd consider it as committing us to a proper version bump.

alternatives.approach: Retain the rfc3986 dependency for parsing and normalization
alternatives.rationale: The author considered the existing integration indirect and awkward in places, and found the internal implementation clearer to understand.

evidence.quote: I think the `rfc3986` package is fantastic, but we were having to do a few bits in some slightly kludgy ways to use it, and without the indirection I find it much clearer to work all the way through what's actually going on here.

candidates.title: Keep overall response timeouts as an unresolved design
candidates.claim: The maintainer expressed interest in total-request timeouts and placed implementation work in httpcore, while recommending async timeout primitives for asyncio and trio. The selected excerpts establish a design direction, not that a total-timeout API shipped.
candidates.scope: Discussion #1450, including the distinction between async cancellation and the synchronous case. No implementation claim is made.

evidence.quote: The implementation for this would be in `httpcore` - I'd be happy to help guide someone through a PR there.
Using async primitives for timeouts is the sensible approach for the `asyncio` and `trio` cases.
Implementing total-request-timeouts would mostly be beneficial for *the sync case*, since there's no cancellation semantics available to us with threaded code.

open_questions: Whether, when, and under which API an overall timeout was implemented is not established here.
